subject: math
title: Linear Relations and Graphs: Interpolation and Extrapolation
seo_title: Grade 9 Linear Relations Worksheets: Graphing, Interpolation and Extrapolation (BC Math, Free)
standard_text: Two-variable linear relations, using graphing, interpolation, and extrapolation
meta_desc: Free Grade 9 math worksheets on linear relations for the BC curriculum: tables of values to graphs, reading graphs, interpolation between points, extrapolation beyond the data, and equations for taxi fares and cooling soup. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Interpolate to find a value between data points. Extrapolate to predict a value beyond them. Both follow the same straight line.
key_sub: A tank has 30 L at 0 hours and 50 L at 2 hours, so it gains 10 L each hour: W = 10t + 30. At 3 hours it holds 60 L (interpolation). It reaches 100 L at 7 hours (extrapolation).
body_html:
From a table of values to a graph

A linear relation changes by the same amount for each step. Its graph is a straight line. To graph it, make a table of values, turn each column into a point (x, y), and plot it: across for x first, then up or down for y.

x0123
y = 2x + 11357

Join the points with a line when every value in between makes sense, like time or distance (continuous). Leave them as separate points for things you count, like tickets or tables (discrete).

Read, interpolate and extrapolate

To read a graph, start on the axis you know, go to the line, then across or down to the other axis. Interpolation finds a value between data points. Extrapolation extends the line to predict a value beyond the data.

Interpolate

A tank has 30 L at 0 hours and 50 L at 2 hours. It fills at a steady rate. How much is in it at 3 hours?

The rate is (50 − 30) ÷ 2 = 10 L each hour. From 2 hours: 50 + 10 = 60.

Answer: 60 L

Extrapolate

The tank keeps filling at the same rate. When does it hold 100 L?

The equation is W = 10t + 30. Solve 10t + 30 = 100: 10t = 70, so t = 7.

Answer: 7 hours

Taxi fare

A taxi charges $4.00 plus $2.00 for each kilometre. What is the equation, and how much is a 7 km ride?

The start fee is the initial value and the cost per kilometre is the rate: C = 2d + 4. For 7 km: 2 × 7 + 4 = 18.

Answer: $18.00

Predictions close to the data are the most reliable. Far beyond the data, the pattern may change: cooling soup stops at room temperature, it does not keep falling forever.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Reading the wrong axis: answering with the x-valueStart on the axis you know and read the answer on the other axis
Plotting (y, x)Go across for x first, then up or down for y
Extrapolating the wrong way: subtracting when going back on a falling lineGoing back, do the opposite of the rate: a falling line gets higher to the left
Taking the nearest data point instead of interpolatingUse the rate to find the exact value between the points
Using the change in y as the rate when x skips numbersDivide the change in y by the change in x
Forgetting the initial value, like a taxi’s start feeAdd the value at x = 0 after multiplying by the rate

faq.q: What do Grade 9 students learn about linear relations in BC?
faq.a: The BC Mathematics 9 curriculum covers two-variable linear relations: making tables of values, graphing them, reading the graphs, and using interpolation and extrapolation to find values between and beyond the data.

faq.q: What is the difference between interpolation and extrapolation?
faq.a: Interpolation finds a value between known data points, such as 3 hours when you have data for 2 and 4 hours. Extrapolation extends the pattern to predict a value outside the data, such as 7 hours when the data stops at 4.

Extrapolation assumes the pattern keeps going in the same way. Far from the data it may not: cooling soup stops at room temperature, so a linear prediction for a long time later can give an impossible answer.

faq.q: How do you write the equation of a linear relation from a word problem?
faq.a: The amount that changes each step is the rate, which multiplies the variable, and the starting amount is the initial value. A taxi that charges $4.00 plus $2.00 per kilometre has C = 2d + 4.

items.q: This table of values is for y = 2x + 1. What value is missing?
items.e: Put x = 3 into the equation: 2 × 3 + 1 = 7. 6 forgets the + 1. 8 adds before multiplying: 2 × (3 + 1). 4 adds 3 + 1 and forgets the 2.

items.q: This table of values is for y = 3x − 2. What value is missing?
items.e: When x = 0, 3 × 0 = 0, so y = 0 − 2 = −2. 2 drops the minus sign. 1 is the value for x = 1. 3 is the constant rate.

items.q: This table of values is for y = −x + 4. What value is missing?
items.e: −(−2) = +2, so y = 2 + 4 = 6. 2 treats −(−2) as −2. 5 is the value for x = −1. −6 makes the whole answer negative.

items.q: Which point do you plot for the column where x = 2?
items.e: Each column gives one point (x, y). For x = 2, y = 11, so plot (2, 11). (11, 2) puts y first. (2, 8) takes y from the column before. (3, 11) uses the wrong x.

items.q: Which graph shows the table x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and y = 1, 3, 5, 7?
items.e: The points are (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7): Graph B. Graph A goes up by 1, not 2. Graph C plots (y, x). Graph D starts at 0 instead of 1.

items.q: For x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, which y-values match the points on the graph?
items.e: Read straight up from each x and across to the y-axis: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14. 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 ignores that the first point is at 2. 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 copies the axis labels. 1, 4, 7, 10, 13 reads one grid line too low.

items.q: For x = 0, 1, 2, 3, which y-values give points on a straight line?
items.e: Points are on a straight line when y changes by the same amount each step. 2, 5, 8, 11 goes up 3 every time. 2, 5, 9, 14 goes up 3, 4, 5. 2, 4, 8, 16 doubles. 1, 4, 9, 16 goes up 3, 5, 7.

items.q: The points (0, 3), (1, 5) and (2, 7) lie on a line. Which point is also on this line?
items.e: y goes up 2 for each 1 in x: (3, 9), then (4, 11). (11, 4) swaps x and y. (4, 9) is one step behind. (3, 8) adds only 1.

items.q: Make a table of values for y = −2x + 1. What is y when x = −3?
items.e: −2 × (−3) = +6, and 6 + 1 = 7. −5 uses −2 × (−3) = −6. 5 subtracts 1 instead of adding. −7 makes both signs negative.

items.q: The table continues in the same way. What is y when x = 8?
items.e: x goes up by 2 and y goes up by 6 each column. The next column is (8, 19 + 6) = 25. 31 adds 6 for each 1 in x: 19 + 2 × 6. 20 adds 1. 24 is 3 × 8 and forgets the start of 1.

items.q: Which relation should be graphed as a solid line, not as separate points?
c: The number of wheels on x bikes
The temperature of soup over time
The number of chairs at x tables
items.e: Time can take any value, like 2.5 minutes, so the temperature of soup over time is continuous: join the points. You cannot buy 2.5 tickets or have 2.5 bikes or tables, so those graphs are separate points (discrete).

items.q: A table of values for y = −3x + 4 is graphed. Which describes the graph?
c: Goes up to the right and crosses the y-axis at −3
Goes down to the right and crosses the y-axis at 4
Goes up to the right and crosses the y-axis at 4
Goes down to the right and crosses the y-axis at −3
items.e: The rate −3 is negative, so y gets smaller as x grows: the line goes down. When x = 0, y = 4. Down to the right, through (0, 4). −3 is the rate, not the start.

items.q: These points should show y = x + 2 for x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Which point is plotted wrong?
items.e: For x = 3, y = 3 + 2 = 5, so the point should be (3, 5). It was plotted at (5, 3): x and y were swapped. The other three points fit the equation.

items.q: Make a table of values for y = 0.5x + 1. What is y when x = 6?
items.e: 0.5 × 6 = 3, and 3 + 1 = 4. 7 adds 6 + 1 and forgets the 0.5. 13 doubles 6 instead of halving it. 3.5 is the value for x = 5.

items.q: Make a table of values for y = −0.5x + 3. What is y when x = 4?
items.e: −0.5 × 4 = −2, and −2 + 3 = 1. 5 uses +2 instead of −2. −5 computes −2 − 3. 2.5 is the value for x = 1.

items.q: Which list of points comes from a table of values for y = 4x − 1?
Where does the graph of y = 2x − 6 cross the y-axis?
items.e: On the y-axis x = 0, and 2 × 0 − 6 = −6. The point is (0, −6). (0, 6) drops the sign. (−6, 0) puts the value on the wrong axis. (3, 0) is where it crosses the x-axis.

items.q: Where does the graph of y = 2x − 6 cross the x-axis?
items.e: On the x-axis y = 0. Solve 2x − 6 = 0: 2x = 6, so x = 3. The point is (3, 0). (0, −6) is the y-axis crossing. (6, 0) forgets to divide by 2. (−3, 0) gets the sign wrong.

items.q: Which graph shows y = −2x + 8 for x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4?
items.e: The points are (0, 8), (1, 6), (2, 4), (3, 2), (4, 0): Graph C. Graph A goes up, but the rate −2 means down. Graph B plots (y, x). Graph D goes down by 1, not 2.

items.q: Which graph shows the table x = 0, 2, 4, 6 and y = 2, 3, 4, 5?
items.e: Plot each column: (0, 2), (2, 3), (4, 4), (6, 5): Graph D. Graph A plots (y, x). Graph B puts the points at x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and ignores that x goes up by 2. Graph C goes up 2 each column instead of 1.

items.q: What is y when x = 4?
items.e: Find 4 on the x-axis, go up to the line, then across to the y-axis: 14. 4 is the x-value, read from the wrong axis. 12 is 3 × 4 without the start of 2. 11 is the value for x = 3.

items.q: For which value of x is y = 8?
items.e: Find 8 on the y-axis, go across to the line, then down: x = 2. 8 is the y-value. 26 puts 8 in for x: 3 × 8 + 2. 6 is 8 − 2 without dividing by 3.

items.q: What is the initial value of this relation (y when x = 0)?
items.e: The line meets the y-axis at 2. 0 guesses that every line starts at the origin. 3 is the rate. 5 is the value for x = 1.

items.q: By how much does y go up each time x goes up by 1?
items.e: (0, 2), (1, 5), (2, 8): each step right, the line goes up 3. 2 is the initial value. 5 is the value at x = 1, not the change. 13 divides the change in x by the change in y.

items.q: The graph shows the height of a cedar seedling. How tall is it after 6 weeks?
items.e: Go up from 6 weeks to the line, then across: 16 cm. 6 is read from the time axis. 12 cm is the growth only (6 × 2) without the 4 cm start. 14 cm is after 5 weeks.

items.q: After how many weeks is the seedling 10 cm tall?
items.e: Find 10 on the height axis, go across to the line, then down: 3 weeks. 10 is the height, not the time. 5 weeks is 10 ÷ 2 and forgets the 4 cm start. 24 puts 10 in for the weeks.

items.q: How much does the seedling grow each week?
items.e: From 4 cm to 6 cm to 8 cm: it grows 2 cm each week. 4 cm is the height at the start. 6 cm is the height after 1 week. 0.5 cm divides the weeks by the centimetres.

items.q: Ji-woo reads the graph and says the seedling is 8 cm tall after 8 weeks. What is the correct height after 8 weeks?
items.e: Go up from 8 weeks to the line and read the height axis: 20 cm. 8 cm comes from reading the time axis instead of the height axis. 16 cm forgets the 4 cm start. 18 cm is after 7 weeks.

items.q: The graph shows the charge on Mei’s phone battery. What is the charge after 4 hours?
items.e: Go up from 4 hours to the line, then across: 50%. 40% is how much charge was used. 4 is read from the time axis. 60% is after 3 hours.

items.q: After how many hours is the charge 30%?
items.e: Find 30 on the charge axis, go across to the line, then down: 6 hours. 3 hours is 30 ÷ 10 and forgets the start of 90%. 12 hours adds: (90 + 30) ÷ 10. 30 is the charge, not the time.

items.q: How much charge does the phone lose each hour?
items.e: 90% to 80% to 70%: it loses 10% each hour. 90% is the charge at the start. 9 is the number of hours until it is empty. 80% is the charge after 1 hour.

items.q: Is this a linear relation?
c: Yes: the charge drops by the same amount each hour
No: the line does not start at 0
items.e: A relation is linear when it changes by the same amount for each step, so its graph is a straight line. Yes: the charge drops 10% every hour. A line can go down and can start anywhere.

items.q: The graph shows the temperature in Prince George after 8:00 p.m. What is the temperature after 5 hours?
items.e: Go up from 5 hours to the line. The point is below the 0 line, at −4 °C. 4 °C forgets the point is below zero. −2 °C is after 4 hours. 16 °C adds 2 °C each hour instead of subtracting.

items.q: At what time does the temperature reach 0 °C?
items.e: The line crosses 0 °C at 3 hours. 3 hours after 8:00 p.m. is 11:00 p.m. 8:00 p.m. is the start, when it is 6 °C. 2:00 a.m. uses the 6 °C as a number of hours. 10:00 p.m. is 2 °C.

items.q: The graph shows Arjun’s savings for a new snowboard. How much has he saved after 4 weeks?
items.e: Go up from 4 weeks to the line, then across: $90. $60 is the money saved in 4 weeks (4 × 15) without the $30 he had at the start. $75 is after 3 weeks. $120 multiplies 4 × 30.

items.q: How much does Arjun save each week?
items.e: Each week the line goes up one grid line: $30, $45, $60. He saves $15 a week. $30 is what he had at the start. $45 is his total after 1 week. $18.75 is 150 ÷ 8 and forgets the $30 start.

items.q: After how many weeks does Arjun have $120?
items.e: Find $120 on the savings axis, go across to the line, then down: 6 weeks. 8 is 120 ÷ 15 and forgets the $30 start. 10 adds: (120 + 30) ÷ 15. 90 is the money saved, not the weeks.

items.q: The point (5, 105) is on the line. What does it mean?
items.e: The first number is on the time axis and the second is on the savings axis: after 5 weeks, Arjun has $105. Swapping them reads the wrong axis.

items.q: The graph shows Liam’s run along the Stanley Park seawall. How far does he run each minute?
items.e: He runs 2 km in 10 minutes. 2 ÷ 10 = 0.2 km each minute. 5 divides the wrong way: 10 ÷ 2 is minutes for each kilometre. 2 km is for 10 minutes, not 1. 0.5 km reads one small grid step on the time axis as 1 minute.

items.q: How many minutes does Liam take to run 5 km?
items.e: Find 5 km on the distance axis, go across to the line, then down: 25 minutes. 5 is the distance. 1 multiplies 5 × 0.2. 20 minutes is the time for 4 km.

items.q: Use the line to find y when x = 3.
items.e: x = 3 is halfway between the points at 2 and 4, so y is halfway between 6 and 10: 8. 6 and 10 just take the nearest plotted point. 3 is the x-value.

items.q: Use the line to find x when y = 12.
items.e: Find 12 on the y-axis, go across to the line and down: 5, halfway between 4 and 6. 12 is the y-value. 4 and 6 stop at a plotted point instead of reading the line.

items.q: The relation is linear. What is y when x = 15?
items.e: y goes up 30 for every 10 in x, so 3 for each 1. From x = 10 to 15: 80 + 5 × 3 = 95. 80 is the nearest value in the table. 45 is 3 × 15 without the start of 50. 125 is the value for x = 25.

items.q: The relation is linear. What is y when x = 5?
items.e: y goes up 6 for every 2 in x, so 3 for each 1. From x = 4: 15 + 3 = 18. 12 subtracts 3, going the wrong way. 15 and 21 are the nearest values in the table.

items.q: A line passes through (2, 7) and (6, 19). What is y at x = 4, halfway between?
items.e: Halfway in x means halfway in y: (7 + 19) ÷ 2 = 13. 26 adds 7 + 19 and forgets to halve. 12 is the change 19 − 7. 4 is the x-value.

items.q: A cup of tea cools at a steady rate. What is its temperature after 6 minutes?
items.e: It cools 16 °C in 4 minutes, so 4 °C each minute. 74 − 2 × 4 = 66 °C. 82 °C adds 8 °C, going the wrong way for cooling tea. 70 °C is after 5 minutes. 62 °C is after 7 minutes.

items.q: A hiker near Whistler climbs at a steady rate. What is the elevation after 1.5 hours?
items.e: 1.5 hours is halfway between 1 and 2 hours, so the elevation is halfway between 800 m and 1000 m: 900 m. 800 m and 1000 m take the nearest plotted point. 300 m is the climb (1.5 × 200) without the 600 m start.

items.q: After how many hours is the hiker at 1100 m?
items.e: 1100 m is halfway between 1000 m (2 hours) and 1200 m (3 hours): 2.5 hours. 2 and 3 hours take the nearest plotted point. 5.5 hours is 1100 ÷ 200 and forgets the 600 m start.

items.q: A linear relation passes through (10, 40) and (20, 25). What is y when x = 14?
items.e: The rate is (25 − 40) ÷ (20 − 10) = −1.5. From x = 10: 40 − 4 × 1.5 = 34. 46 adds 6, going the wrong way. 32.5 is halfway, but 14 is not halfway between 10 and 20. 19 takes 6 from 25, the wrong end.

items.q: A table shows a plant’s height every week from week 0 to week 10. Which question uses interpolation?
c: How tall was it in week 7.5?
How tall will it be in week 15?
How tall was it before week 0?
items.e: Interpolation finds values between the data. Week 7.5 is between week 0 and week 10. Week 15, before week 0, and a height past the data are extrapolation.

items.q: The relation is linear. What value is missing?
items.e: x = 3 is halfway between 0 and 6, so y is halfway between 5 and 17: 11. 8 adds the x-step 3 to 5. 12 is the change 17 − 5. 14 takes 3 from 17.

items.q: Rain fills a barrel in Vancouver at a steady rate. How much water is in it after 2.5 hours?
items.e: It gains 40 L in 4 hours, so 10 L each hour. 20 + 2.5 × 10 = 45 L. 40 L is after 2 hours. 25 L is 2.5 × 10 without the 20 L start. 50 L is after 3 hours.

items.q: After how many hours does the barrel hold 35 L?
items.e: It must gain 35 − 20 = 15 L at 10 L each hour: 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 hours. 3.5 hours is 35 ÷ 10 and forgets the 20 L start. 1 and 2 hours round to a whole hour.

items.q: Why can you interpolate between two data points of a linear relation?
c: The values between them lie on the same straight line
items.e: In a linear relation the rate is constant, so every value between two points lies on the same straight line. Lines can start anywhere, can go down, and can use any x between the points.

items.q: A line passes through (−2, 9) and (2, 1). What is y when x = 1?
items.e: The rate is (1 − 9) ÷ (2 − (−2)) = −8 ÷ 4 = −2. From (2, 1), go back 1: 1 + 2 = 3. 5 is the value at x = 0. 7 moves the wrong way from (−2, 9). −1 is the value for x = 3.

items.q: A line passes through (0, 3) and (4, 5). What is y when x = 3?
items.e: The rate is (5 − 3) ÷ 4 = 0.5. 3 + 3 × 0.5 = 4.5. 9 uses the rate 4 ÷ 2 = 2, divided the wrong way. 4 is the halfway value, but 3 is not halfway. 5 is the value at x = 4.

items.q: The relation is linear. For which value of x is y = 158?
items.e: y goes down 6 for each 1 in x. From 200 to 158 is 42: 42 ÷ 6 = 7. 2 starts from 170 but forgets that 170 is at x = 5. 8 is how far back from x = 15, not the x-value. 6 is one step short.

items.q: Soup is 70 °C after 2 minutes and 54 °C after 6 minutes. It cools at a steady rate. What is its temperature after 5 minutes?
items.e: It cools 16 °C in 4 minutes, so 4 °C each minute. 70 − 3 × 4 = 58 °C. 62 °C is the halfway value, after 4 minutes. 82 °C adds 12 °C, the wrong way for cooling soup. 50 °C goes from 54 °C the wrong way: back in time it should be warmer.

items.q: A graph shows the number of chairs, y, around x tables. Why should you not interpolate at x = 2.5?
c: 2.5 is too far from the data
You cannot have half a table
items.e: Tables come in whole numbers, so the relation is discrete. Interpolate only where the in-between values make sense. There is no half a table.

items.q: In Kelowna it is 12 °C at 9:00 a.m. and 24 °C at 1:00 p.m. The temperature rises at a steady rate. What is the temperature at 10:00 a.m.?
items.e: From 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. is 4 hours, so it rises 12 ÷ 4 = 3 °C each hour. 12 + 3 = 15 °C. 18 °C is the halfway value, at 11:00 a.m. 13 °C adds 1 °C. 21 °C is at 12:00 p.m.

items.q: The relation continues in the same way. What is y when x = 7?
items.e: y goes up 2 each step: 11, 13, 15, 17. Or use y = 2x + 3: 2 × 7 + 3 = 17. 14 is 2 × 7 without the start of 3. 15 is the value for x = 6 and 19 is for x = 8.

items.q: Extend the table to the left. What is y when x = −2?
items.e: Going left, y goes down 2 each step: 3, 1, −1. 7 adds 2 each step, going the wrong way. 1 is the value for x = −1. −4 is 2 × (−2) without the start of 3.

items.q: The pattern continues past the grid. What is y when x = 9?
items.e: The points go up 2 each step from 2, so y = 2x + 2. For x = 9: 2 × 9 + 2 = 20. 18 forgets the start of 2. 22 is the value for x = 10. 10 is the last point on the grid.

items.q: The relation continues in the same way. What is y when x = 8?
items.e: y goes down 5 each step: 40 − 8 × 5 = 0. 65 adds 5 each step, going the wrong way. 5 is the value for x = 7 and −5 is for x = 9.

items.q: Extend the table back to x = 0. What is y?
items.e: Going back, the values go up 3 each step: 14, 17, 20. 8 subtracts 3 twice, going the wrong way. 17 is the value for x = 1 and 23 is for x = −1.

items.q: A table shows a plant’s height every week from week 0 to week 10. Which question uses extrapolation?
c: How tall will it be in week 15?
How tall was it in week 10?
How tall was it in week 4?
How tall was it in week 7.5?
items.e: Extrapolation predicts values beyond the data. Week 15 is past week 10. Weeks 4, 7.5 and 10 are inside the data.

items.q: Tea is 90 °C. Ava measures it for 5 minutes: 90, 87, 84, 81, 78, 75 °C. If it keeps cooling at this rate, what is its temperature after 10 minutes?
items.e: It cools 3 °C each minute: 90 − 10 × 3 = 60 °C. 120 °C adds, the wrong way for cooling tea. 63 °C is after 9 minutes. 30 °C is 10 × 3, the drop only.

items.q: Tea at 90 °C cools 3 °C each minute for the first 5 minutes. A linear model predicts −30 °C after 40 minutes. Why is this prediction wrong?
c: Tea stops cooling near room temperature
The tea should be warmer than 90 °C
items.e: Real tea cools to about room temperature and then stays there. Extrapolating far beyond the data can give impossible answers. The linear pattern only holds for a while. Outdoor temperatures in BC can be below 0 °C.

items.q: Extend the pattern back to x = 0. What is y?
items.e: Each step right adds 2, so each step left takes away 2: 7, 5, 3. 11 adds 2 twice, going the wrong way. 5 is the value for x = 1. 7 is the first plotted point.

items.q: Snow on a deck in Kamloops melts at a steady rate. On which day will the snow be gone?
items.e: It melts 4 cm a day. On day 3 there is 24 cm left: 24 ÷ 4 = 6 more days, so day 3 + 6 = day 9. 8 is 32 ÷ 4 and forgets the table starts at day 1. 6 is the number of days after day 3. 10 is one day too many.

items.q: Owen saves the same amount each week. If he keeps saving, how much will he have after 10 weeks?
items.e: He saves $15 a week. From week 5 to week 10 is 5 weeks: 85 + 5 × 15 = $160. $170 doubles the week 5 amount, but he started with money. $145 is week 9. $150 is 10 × 15 and forgets his start.

items.q: How much did Owen have at the start (week 0)?
items.e: Going back, take away $15 each week: 55 − 3 × 15 = $10. $100 adds $45, going the wrong way. $40 goes back only one week. $0 assumes he started with nothing.

items.q: The temperature keeps falling at the same rate. What is it after 5 hours?
items.e: It falls 3 °C each hour: 0, −3, −6 °C. 6 °C forgets the sign below zero. −3 °C is after 4 hours. 24 °C adds 3 °C each hour, the wrong way.

items.q: The pattern continues. For which value of x is y = −8?
items.e: The points go down 2 each step from 4: y = −2x + 4. Solve −2x + 4 = −8: −2x = −12, so x = 6. −2 goes left, the wrong way: there y = 8. 4 is −8 ÷ (−2) and forgets the start of 4. 12 forgets to divide by 2.

items.q: Data for a linear relation goes from x = 0 to x = 10. Which prediction is most reliable?
items.e: The closer a prediction is to the data, the more you can trust it. x = 11 is just past the data. Far beyond the data, the pattern may change.

items.q: A line passes through (4, 10) and (6, 16). What is y when x = 10?
items.e: The rate is (16 − 10) ÷ (6 − 4) = 3. From (6, 16): 16 + 4 × 3 = 28. 25 assumes the line goes through (0, 0): 10 × 2.5. 22 is the value for x = 8 and 34 is for x = 12.

items.q: A line passes through (4, 10) and (6, 16). What is y when x = 0?
items.e: Going back, take away 3 for each step: 10 − 4 × 3 = −2. 22 adds 12, going the wrong way. 4 goes back only 2 steps. 10 is the value at x = 4.

items.q: A candle is 30 cm tall. Chloe records its height for 4 hours: 30, 28.5, 27, 25.5, 24 cm. If it keeps burning at this rate, after how many hours will it be 6 cm tall?
items.e: It burns 1.5 cm each hour. It must lose 30 − 6 = 24 cm: 24 ÷ 1.5 = 16 hours. 4 hours is 6 ÷ 1.5. 20 hours is when it is all gone. 24 is the centimetres lost, not the hours.

items.q: Mateo’s family drives on the Trans-Canada Highway at a steady speed. If they keep this speed, how far will they go in 5 hours?
items.e: They drive 90 km each hour: 5 × 90 = 450 km. 270 km is the last point on the graph. 360 km is after 4 hours. 540 km doubles the 3-hour distance, which is 6 hours.

items.q: Nadia extends the table back to x = 1 and gets y = 14. What is the correct value?
items.e: Going forward, y goes down 3. Going back, it goes up 3: 20, 23, 26. Nadia subtracted 6, extrapolating the wrong way. 23 is the value for x = 2. 17 is in the table at x = 4.

items.q: A taxi charges $4.00 to start plus $2.00 for each kilometre. Which equation gives the cost, C, in dollars, for d kilometres?
items.e: Each kilometre adds $2, so 2 multiplies d. The $4 is paid once: C = 2d + 4. C = 4d + 2 swaps the start fee and the rate. C = 6d charges $6 for every kilometre. C = 2d forgets the start fee.

items.q: A taxi costs C = 2d + 4 dollars for d km. How much is a 7 km ride?
items.e: C = 2 × 7 + 4 = 14 + 4 = $18.00. $42.00 adds first: (2 + 4) × 7. $14.00 forgets the start fee. $30.00 swaps the numbers: 4 × 7 + 2.

items.q: A taxi costs C = 2d + 4 dollars for d km. Kai pays $25.00. How long was the ride?
items.e: Solve 2d + 4 = 25. Subtract 4: 2d = 21. Divide by 2: d = 10.5 km. 12.5 km is 25 ÷ 2 and forgets the start fee. 14.5 km adds the fee. 21 km forgets to divide.

items.q: The graph shows the taxi fare. What does the point where the line meets the cost axis show?
c: The cost of an 8 km ride
The $4.00 paid before the taxi moves
items.e: At 0 km the cost is already $4. That is the start fee, paid before the taxi moves. The cost for each kilometre is the rate, $2.

items.q: Soup is 84 °C and cools 3 °C each minute. Which equation gives its temperature, T, in °C, after m minutes?
items.e: The soup starts at 84 °C and loses 3 °C a minute, so the rate is −3: T = −3m + 84. T = 3m + 84 makes the soup get hotter. T = 84m − 3 swaps the rate and the start. T = −3m + 81 starts from the temperature after 1 minute.

items.q: Soup cools by the rule T = −3m + 84. What is its temperature after 6 minutes?
items.e: T = −3 × 6 + 84 = −18 + 84 = 66 °C. 102 °C adds the 18 degrees, but soup cools. 18 °C is the drop only. 69 °C is after 5 minutes.

items.q: Soup cools by the rule T = −3m + 84. After how many minutes is it 60 °C?
items.e: Solve −3m + 84 = 60. It must cool 84 − 60 = 24 °C: 24 ÷ 3 = 8 minutes. 20 is 60 ÷ 3 and forgets the start. 24 is degrees, not minutes. 48 adds: (84 + 60) ÷ 3.

items.q: In the taxi rule C = 2.25d + 3.75, what does 2.25 mean?
c: The total cost of the ride
The cost before the ride starts
items.e: 2.25 multiplies the distance, so it is the rate: $2.25 for each kilometre. $3.75 is the start fee, paid before the ride. The total depends on d.

items.q: Taxi A charges $4.00 plus $2.00 per km. Taxi B charges $6.00 plus $1.50 per km. Which is cheaper for a 10 km ride?
items.e: Taxi A: 2 × 10 + 4 = $24.00. Taxi B: 1.5 × 10 + 6 = $21.00. Taxi B is cheaper by $3.00. They cost the same only at 4 km. $0.50 is the difference in rates for 1 km.

items.q: A 3 km taxi ride costs $11.50 and a 7 km ride costs $21.50. The cost is linear. Which equation gives the cost, C, for d km?
items.e: The rate is (21.50 − 11.50) ÷ (7 − 3) = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5. Start fee: 11.50 − 3 × 2.5 = 4. C = 2.5d + 4. C = 2.5d forgets the start fee. C = 4d + 2.5 swaps the rate and the fee. C = 10d + 4 uses the $10 change without dividing by 4 km.

items.q: Taxi A charges $4.00 plus $2.00 per km. Taxi B charges $6.00 plus $1.50 per km. For what distance do they cost the same?
items.e: Set them equal: 2d + 4 = 1.5d + 6. Then 0.5d = 2, so d = 4 km. Both cost $12. 2 km is the difference in start fees. 12 is the cost. 0.5 is the difference in rates.

items.q: Which equation matches the cooling coffee? (T is the temperature and m is minutes.)
items.e: It loses 8 °C every 2 minutes, so 4 °C each minute. It starts at 80 °C: T = −4m + 80. T = 4m + 80 gets hotter. T = −8m + 80 uses the change for 2 minutes as the rate. T = −4m + 72 starts at the second point.

items.q: If the coffee keeps cooling at this rate, after how many minutes will it be 40 °C?
items.e: Solve −4m + 80 = 40: it must cool 40 °C, and 40 ÷ 4 = 10 minutes. 5 uses 8 °C per minute. 40 is read from the temperature axis. 12 goes one step of 2 minutes too far.

items.q: Ryan rents a kayak in Nanaimo for $15.00 plus $10.00 an hour. How much does he pay for 2.5 hours?
Simran’s class has $80 for the Terry Fox Run and raises $40 more each week. After how many weeks will they have $400?
items.e: Solve 40w + 80 = 400. 400 − 80 = 320 and 320 ÷ 40 = 8 weeks. 10 is 400 ÷ 40 and forgets the $80. 12 adds: (400 + 80) ÷ 40. 320 forgets to divide.

items.q: At 2:00 p.m. a pot of soup is 90 °C. At 2:10 p.m. it is 70 °C. It cools at a steady rate. By how much does the temperature change each minute?
items.e: (70 − 90) ÷ 10 = −20 ÷ 10 = −2 °C each minute. 2 °C forgets that the soup is cooling. −20 °C is the change in 10 minutes. −0.5 divides the wrong way.

items.q: A 5 km taxi ride costs $16.25 and an 8 km ride costs $23.00. The cost is linear. What is the start fee?
items.e: The rate is (23.00 − 16.25) ÷ 3 = $2.25 per km. Go back 5 km from $16.25: 16.25 − 5 × 2.25 = $5.00. $27.50 adds, extrapolating the wrong way. $14.00 goes back only 1 km. $6.75 is the change between the rides.

items.q: Zara is 340 km from home and drives toward home at 80 km/h. After how many hours is she 100 km from home?
items.e: Solve 340 − 80t = 100. She must drive 240 km: 240 ÷ 80 = 3 hours. 1.25 hours is 100 ÷ 80. 5.5 hours adds: (340 + 100) ÷ 80. 4.25 hours is the whole trip home.

items.q: Which situation matches y = −5x + 60?
c: A tank holds 5 L and drains 60 L each minute
A tank holds 5 L and fills 60 L each minute
A tank holds 60 L and fills 5 L each minute
A tank holds 60 L and drains 5 L each minute
items.e: 60 is the initial value: the tank starts with 60 L. The rate −5 means it loses 5 L each minute. It holds 60 L and drains 5 L each minute.

items.q: A taxi charges $4.00 plus $2.00 per km. Chloe pays $27.00, which includes a $3.00 tip. How long was the ride?
items.e: Take off the tip: 27 − 3 = $24. Solve 2d + 4 = 24: 2d = 20, so d = 10 km. 11.5 km forgets the tip. 13.5 km is 27 ÷ 2. 12 km forgets the $4 start fee.
